passages.text: Bicuspid aortic valve formation: <italic>Nos3</italic> mutation leads to abnormal lineage patterning of neural crest cells and the second heart field
ABSTRACT

The bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), a valve with two instead of three aortic leaflets, belongs to the most prevalent congenital heart diseases in the world, occurring in 0.5-2% of the general population. <sentence_start/>We aimed to understand how changes in early cellular contributions result in BAV formation and impact cardiovascular outflow tract development. <sentence_start/>Detailed 3D reconstructions, immunohistochemistry and morphometrics determined that, during valvulogenesis, the non-coronary leaflet separates from the parietal outflow tract cushion instead of originating from an intercalated cushion. <sentence_start/><italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice develop a BAV without a raphe as a result of incomplete separation of the parietal outflow tract cushion into the right and non-coronary leaflet. <sentence_start/>Genetic lineage tracing of endothelial, second heart field and neural crest cells revealed altered deposition of neural crest cells and second heart field cells within the parietal outflow tract cushion of <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos. <sentence_start/>The abnormal cell lineage distributions also affected the positioning of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the orifice level. <sentence_start/>The results demonstrate that the development of the right and non-coronary leaflets are closely related. <sentence_start/>A small deviation in the distribution of neural crest and second heart field populations affects normal valve formation and results in the predominant right-non-type BAV in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice.

<bold>Summary:</bold> The endothelial <italic>Nos3</italic> mutation impacts neural-crest and second-heart-field lineage patterning within the aortic valve, which affects outflow-tract formation, as well as aortopulmonary angulation.
INTRODUCTION

The tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) has a crucial role in maintaining unidirectional blood flow from the left ventricle into the systemic circulation. <sentence_start/>Abnormalities in aortic valve morphology, as seen in the case of the bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), have been linked to valvular regurgitation, stenosis and progressive thoracic aortic aneurysm development (<citation rid="DMM034637C50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/heart.83.1.81" pmid="10618341" pmcid="PMC1729267" count="1">Ward, 2000</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMra1207059" pmid="24827036" count="1">Verma and Siu, 2014</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/ejcts/ezv087" pmid="25787670" count="1">Sievers et al., 2015</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.amjcard.2017.03.245" pmid="28483205" count="1">Merkx et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>A BAV is currently accepted as a congenital anomaly with a high incidence, occurring in 0.5-2% of the Western population (<citation rid="DMM034637C36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0002-9149(70)90761-7" pmid="5427836" count="1">Roberts, 1970</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/heart.83.1.81" pmid="10618341" pmcid="PMC1729267" count="1">Ward, 2000</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0735-1097(02)01886-7" pmid="12084585" count="1">Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002</citation>).

BAV formation is generally considered to be an abnormal fusion of aortic leaflets occurring during embryonic development (<citation rid="DMM034637C9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jacc.2009.07.044" pmid="19958967" count="1">Fernández et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.acvd.2015.10.002" pmid="26711547" count="1">Théron et al., 2015</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.151944" pmid="29158447" count="1">Odelin et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although leaflet fusion might be a valid mechanistic explanation, there are currently no unequivocal data supporting this mechanism in BAV mouse models.

During embryonic development the heart starts as a single heart tube consisting of an outer layer of myocardium and an inner lining of endocardium. <sentence_start/>These layers are separated by a thick hydrophilic region of cardiac jelly, rich in extracellular matrix, hyaluronic acid, glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans, produced by cardiomyocytes (<citation rid="DMM034637C26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jmor.1051250306" pmid="5678904" count="1">Manasek, 1968</citation>). <sentence_start/>The primitive myocardium secretes factors, such as Bmp2, in the cardiac jelly that induce the transition of endothelial cells into mesenchymal cells (EMT) (<citation rid="DMM034637C43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2004.01.045" pmid="15110716" count="1">Sugi et al., 2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>This process results in an invasion of endothelial-derived mesenchymal cells into the cardiac jelly (<citation rid="DMM034637C7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.RES.77.1.1" pmid="7788867" count="1">Eisenberg and Markwald, 1995</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.2000.0106" pmid="11161575" count="1">Kisanuki et al., 2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the cardiac outflow tract (OFT), EMT results in the formation of a septal and a parietal cushion, the primordia of the myocardial OFT septum and the semilunar valves. <sentence_start/>Defects in cardiac jelly synthesis result in severely hypoplastic cushions due to failed EMT (<citation rid="DMM034637C3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.RES.74.2.244" pmid="8293563" count="1">Baldwinet al., 1994</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI10272" pmid="10930438" pmcid="PMC314332" count="1">Camenisch et al., 2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>Failure of EMT has been shown to result in BAVs (<citation rid="DMM034637C45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035539" pmid="22536403" pmcid="PMC3334911" count="1">Thomas et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/cvr/cvv040" pmid="25691540" pmcid="PMC4362403" count="1">Mommersteeg et al., 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>BAV formation in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> has also been suggested to be caused by early defects in EMT resulting in reduced mesenchyme populations in the OFT cushions (<citation rid="DMM034637C9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jacc.2009.07.044" pmid="19958967" count="1">Fernández et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0077611" pmid="24204893" pmcid="PMC3812218" count="1">Liu et al., 2013</citation>).

Migration of cardiac neural crest cells from the neuroectoderm into the OFT cushions induces the formation of the aortopulmonary (AP) septum, which divides the common OFT at the cardiac-to-vascular border into an aortic and pulmonary orifice, and more proximally located intracardiac tissue into a right and left ventricular OFT (<citation rid="DMM034637C48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.1998.8860" pmid="9576827" count="1">Waldo et al., 1998</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10725237" doi="10.1242/dev.127.8.1607" count="1">Jiang et al., 2000</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1203/01.PDR.0000148710.69159.61" pmid="15611355" count="1">Gittenberger-De Groot et al., 2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>During further development, the parietal cushion gives rise to, at the orifice level, the right-facing leaflets of the aortic and the pulmonary valve, while the septal cushion will develop into the left-facing leaflets of both valves. <sentence_start/>Finally, the non-facing aortic leaflet and pulmonary leaflet are considered to be derived from separately developing intercalated cushions on the posterior and anterior sides of the OFT, respectively (<citation rid="DMM034637C19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/aja.1000710303" count="1">Kramer, 1942</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.063495" pmid="22912411" pmcid="PMC3424040" count="1">Lin et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although the development of the septal and parietal cushion has been studied intensively, the role of these intercalated cushions during development remains a challenging concept despite recent progress (<citation rid="DMM034637C2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/heart.89.9.1110" pmid="12923046" pmcid="PMC1767864" count="1">Anderson et al., 2003</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.063495" pmid="22912411" pmcid="PMC3424040" count="1">Lin et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.34110" pmcid="PMC6025960" pmid="29956664" count="1">Eley et al., 2018</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.24641" pmid="29920846" pmcid="PMC6105448" count="1">Mifflin et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>For clarity of description of the valve leaflets and the correlation with the terminology used for the aortic leaflets in human patients with BAV, we will refer to the aortic leaflets as right coronary (RC), left coronary (LC) and non-coronary (NC) leaflets (<citation rid="DMM034637C41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jtcvs.2007.01.039" pmid="17467434" count="1">Sievers and Schmidtke, 2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>For the pulmonary semilunar valve leaflets we have chosen to use right-facing (RF), left-facing (LF) and a non-facing (NF) leaflets (Fig. 1A-D).

It is well established that the aorta and aortic valve are developmentally related. <sentence_start/>Neural crest (<citation rid="DMM034637C48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.1998.8860" pmid="9576827" count="1">Waldo et al., 1998</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="10725237" doi="10.1242/dev.127.8.1607" count="1">Jiang et al., 2000</citation>), endothelial (<citation rid="DMM034637C7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.RES.77.1.1" pmid="7788867" count="1">Eisenberg and Markwald, 1995</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1006/dbio.2000.0106" pmid="11161575" count="1">Kisanuki et al., 2001</citation>), epicardial cell lineages (<citation rid="DMM034637C11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.diff.2012.05.002" pmid="22652098" count="1">Gittenberger-de Groot et al., 2012</citation>) and second heart field (SHF) (<citation rid="DMM034637C52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.diff.2012.03.003" pmid="22521611" count="1">Zaffran and Kelly, 2012</citation>)-derived cells contribute to both the ascending aorta, the aortic valve (<citation rid="DMM034637C8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.34110" pmcid="PMC6025960" pmid="29956664" count="1">Eley et al., 2018</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.24641" pmid="29920846" pmcid="PMC6105448" count="1">Mifflin et al., 2018</citation>) and the various components of the aortic root (valvular leaflets, annulus, sinuses of Valsalva) (<citation rid="DMM034637C6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="885781" pmcid="PMC1234725" count="1">de la Cruz et al., 1977</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.6844926" pmid="6844926" count="1">Kirby et al., 1983</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C49" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11688566" doi="10.1242/dev.128.16.3179" count="1">Waldo et al., 2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>Mouse models of BAVs show cushion formation to be an essential process during valve formation, and defects in the contributing cell lineages are known to result in BAVs (<citation rid="DMM034637C4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.RES.87.10.888" pmid="11073884" count="1">Biben et al., 2000</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/01.CIR.101.20.2345" pmid="10821808" count="1">Lee et al., 2000</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.00850" pmid="14623825" pmcid="PMC1876660" count="1">Macatee, 2003</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ydbio.2011.07.037" pmid="21839733" count="1">Laforest and Nemer, 2011</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddr434" pmid="21940751" pmcid="PMC3235008" count="1">Makki and Capecchi, 2012</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0035539" pmid="22536403" pmcid="PMC3334911" count="1">Thomas et al., 2012</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/cvr/cvv040" pmid="25691540" pmcid="PMC4362403" count="1">Mommersteeg et al., 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the present study, we examined the contributions of neural crest, endothelial and SHF lineages in aortic valve development of wild-type and <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mouse embryos to identify novel congenital aberrations involved in the formation of a BAV. <sentence_start/>Understanding the fundamental embryology of these early cardiac lineages is crucial to address the challenges in BAV pathology.
RESULTS
Morphological landmarks in bicuspid <italic>Nos3</italic><sup>−/−</sup> mice

Seventy-three percent of <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos had a normal TAV, while 27% develop a BAV (Table S4). <sentence_start/>In <italic>Nos3</italic><sup>−/−</sup> embryos, the BAV had two similarly sized leaflets in a left-right leaflet orientation without a visible raphe that indicated the position of a possible third commissure (Fig. 1A,B). <sentence_start/>The lack of a raphe did not allow for discrimination between an R-N (a fusion/confluence of RC and NC leaflets)- or L-N (a fusion/confluence of LC and NC leaflets)-type BAV solely on the basis of morphological aspects. <sentence_start/>In wild-type mice, the three parabolic-shaped leaflets are embedded within the aortic root. <sentence_start/>Distally, at the sinotubular junction, these structures formed three interleaflet commissures. <sentence_start/>In contrast to wild type, bicuspid <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice developed a commissure (arrowheads, Fig. 1A,B) opposite to the facing commissure (arrow, Fig. 1A,B). <sentence_start/>Fig. 1.

Incomplete separation of the parietal cushion leads to an R-N BAV in <italic>Nos3</italic><sup>−/−</sup> embryos

The first indications of leaflet formation could be observed at E12.0, at which point the putative aortic valve leaflets consisted of the parietal and septal cushions and a slight indentation of endothelial cells was present in both wild-type and <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos (Fig. 1E,F, arrowheads). <sentence_start/>At E12.5, a marked separation of the parietal cushion was observed in wild-type embryos. <sentence_start/>The RC and NC leaflet could be distinguished by the presence of an endothelial infolding into the cushion (Fig. 1G, arrowhead). <sentence_start/>Bicuspid <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos did not develop this marked endothelial infolding, causing an incomplete separation of the parietal cushion into an NC and RC leaflet (Fig. 1H). <sentence_start/>This resulted in the formation of a single right valvular leaflet, leading to an R-N BAV. <sentence_start/>Moreover, there was no indication of intercalated cushion development in wild-type embryos between the parietal and septal cushion between E10.5 and E12.5 (Fig. S1).
Aortic leaflets develop solely from the parietal and septal cushions

The early OFT cushion formation started around E10.5 in wild-type mice with the production of cardiac jelly within the interstitial space between the outer myocardial wall and inner endocardial lining, followed by migration of endocardial-derived cells into two compartments, resulting in the two OFT cushions: the parietal and septal cushions (Fig. S1). <sentence_start/>During cellularization the two cushions remained interconnected by two thin transitional zones. <sentence_start/>The transitional zones are two distinct regions which connect the parietal and septal cushion over the complete length at both ends and are characterized by their composition of mostly cardiac jelly, virtually devoid of cells (Fig. 2A, Fig. S1). <sentence_start/>At E10.5 and E11.0, the parietal cushion was positioned ventrolaterally in the cardiac OFT, whereas the septal cushion was located more dorsomedially (Fig. 2A,B). <sentence_start/>Extracardiac SHF cells could be observed immunohistochemically as non-myocardial [tropomyosin (TM) negative] cells expressing nuclear NKX2.5 (<citation rid="DMM034637C49" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11688566" doi="10.1242/dev.128.16.3179" count="1">Waldo et al., 2001</citation>) (Fig. S2). <sentence_start/>NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cells (Fig. 2, Fig. S3; yellow) migrated via the pharyngeal arteries into the distal parts of the parietal and septal cushions into the cardiac OFT (Fig. 2, Fig. S3; orange). <sentence_start/>From E11.5 onwards, the future pulmonary OFT changed from a left medial position to a more ventral position with regard to the future aortic ostium, corresponding to a clockwise rotation (Fig. 2C-E, Fig. S3C-E). <sentence_start/>This phenomenon has been described as resulting from the asymmetric addition of SHF cells to the pulmonary side of the OFT, the so-called ‘pulmonary push’ (<citation rid="DMM034637C38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.23833" pmid="22826212" count="1">Scherptong et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>The parietal cushion became positioned more dorsal and the septal cushion more ventral (Fig. 2D,E). <sentence_start/>At this stage, the NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cells form a distinct group of cells in the septal and parietal cushions close to the transitional zones (Fig. 2D,E; cyan, Fig. S3D,E). <sentence_start/>The transitional zones in between the septal and parietal cushions remained sparsely populated by cells. <sentence_start/>The interleaflet commissures of the LC and NC aortic leaflets as well as the LF and NF pulmonary leaflets developed at these transitional zones. <sentence_start/>The pulmonary NF leaflet also derived from a main OFT cushion (in this case, the septal cushion). <sentence_start/>The timing is somewhat different in that this occurred at E12.0 (Fig. 2D), whilst the separation of the aortic NC leaflet from the parietal cushion occurred somewhat later, at E12.5 (Fig. 2E). <sentence_start/>The septal cushion therefore gave rise to three leaflets: the LC aortic leaflet as well as the LF and NF pulmonary leaflets. <sentence_start/>The parietal cushion also gave rise to three leaflets: the RC and NC aortic leaflets as well as the RF pulmonary leaflet (Fig. 2E). <sentence_start/>Fig. 2.

The volume of the myocardium and the OFT cushions are not affected in <italic>Nos3</italic><sup>−/−</sup> embryos

Developmental growth of the OFT cushions could be determined by a decrease in acellular fraction volume (as a measure for the amount of cardiac jelly) and an increase in cellular fraction volume containing cell bodies. <sentence_start/>Histological image examination determined no difference (<italic>P</italic>>0.05) in cushion composition of the septal and parietal cushions between <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> and wild-type embryos from stages E10.5-E12.5 (Fig. S4A-B). <sentence_start/>These findings indicate that defects in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos were not caused due to a reduction in total cell volume or changes in cardiac jelly production. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, no differences were found in heart size based on ventricular myocardial volume measurements between wild type and <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos at embryonic age E10.5-E13.5 indicating that the myocardial growth rate is unaffected by the <italic>Nos3</italic> mutation (Fig. S4C).
Aortic and pulmonary leaflets harbour unique cell lineage distributions

The use of the Cre-<italic>loxP</italic> system allowed the study of cellular offspring by genetically labelling original progenitor cells (<citation rid="DMM034637C37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.85.14.5166" pmid="2839833" pmcid="PMC281709" count="1">Sauer and Henderson, 1988</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/(SICI)1526-968X(200002)26:2<99::AID-GENE1>3.0.CO;2-B" pmid="10686599" count="1">Nagy, 2000</citation>). <sentence_start/>By combining genetic lineage tracing and antibody staining it was confirmed that the NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> population within the NC leaflets of the aorta are of SHF descent and that these do not colocalize with endothelial (Fig. S5A) or neural-crest (Fig. S5B)-derived populations, but are a subpopulation of the <italic>Mef2c</italic>-derived SHF cells (Fig. S5C). <sentence_start/>These NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF populations are also found in the NF leaflet in the pulmonary orifice (Fig. S5D-F). <sentence_start/>Recently, studies by Mifflin et al. and Eley et al. have identified similar populations in the NC leaflet of the aorta (<citation rid="DMM034637C8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.34110" pmcid="PMC6025960" pmid="29956664" count="1">Eley et al., 2018</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.24641" pmid="29920846" pmcid="PMC6105448" count="1">Mifflin et al., 2018</citation>).

Cell lineage image quantification determined specific regions in the aortic valve to which early cardiac cell lineages contributed. <sentence_start/>In wild-type embryos, the majority of NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cells contributed to the NC leaflet (Fig. 3A,D), whereas cells of neural crest origin primarily contributed to the LC and RC leaflets (Fig. 3C,F). <sentence_start/>Similar neural crest patterns have also been reported in other studies (<citation rid="DMM034637C32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/cvr/cvt132" pmid="23723064" pmcid="PMC3718324" count="1">Phillips et al., 2013</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.151944" pmid="29158447" count="1">Odelin et al., 2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, endothelial-derived cells were equally distributed among the aortic leaflets in wild-type embryos (Fig. 3B,E). <sentence_start/>Fig. 3.

DISCUSSION

Patients with a BAV are at an increased risk of developing aortopathy. <sentence_start/>The great vessels and the aortic valve have a similar developmental origin involving contributions of endothelial, neural crest and SHF lineages. <sentence_start/>Understanding the exact role of these early cell lineages during leaflet development and OFT formation may lead to more accurate patient risk stratification and improved treatment strategies.

In this study, the formation of the aortic valve in wild-type and <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mouse embryos was studied to identify congenital cell lineage aberrations involved in the formation of bicuspid aortic valves. <sentence_start/>To the best of our knowledge, we describe for the first time that the NF leaflets of the aortic and pulmonary valves arise from a process of cushion separation of the parietal and septal cushions during development. <sentence_start/>This finding contradicts previous studies, which argued that the formation of the NF leaflets developed from separate intercalated cushions (<citation rid="DMM034637C19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/aja.1000710303" count="1">Kramer, 1942</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C34" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Anderson et al., 2003</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.063495" pmid="22912411" pmcid="PMC3424040" count="1">Lin et al., 2012</citation>; <citation doi="10.1002/dvdy.24641" pmid="29920846" pmcid="PMC6105448" count="1">Mifflin et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>The morphological events leading to semilunar valve formation is a challenging concept to represent in a 2D-plane due to complex 3D OFT remodelling. <sentence_start/>Interpretations based on 2D histological sections may result in an incomplete view of the morphological changes throughout development. <sentence_start/>Moreover, these rapid morphological changes require short intervals in between observations and 3D reconstructions for accurate representations of the complete cushions within the context of the cardiac OFT remodelling during embryogenesis. <sentence_start/>The process of leaflet separation requires formation of endothelial infolding within the cushion. <sentence_start/>Fernández et al. reported fusion of the NC and RC (R-N BAV) as the underlying mechanism for BAV in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice (<citation rid="DMM034637C9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jacc.2009.07.044" pmid="19958967" count="1">Fernández et al., 2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the absence of a strand of opposed endothelial cells that runs from the lumen to the sinus wall in the parietal cushion shows that the developmental background of the R-N BAV is not the result of a fusion process between two OFT cushions, but rather the result of an incomplete or absent separation process of the RC and NC leaflets from the parietal cushion during early valve development. <sentence_start/>We therefore found no indications of endothelial opposition that could support the theory of direct fusion. <sentence_start/>Recently, Eley and colleagues linked the formation of BAV without a raphe to deficiencies in arterial valve cells from <italic>Mef2c-AHF-Cre<sup>+</sup>/Tnnt2-Cre<sup>+</sup></italic> progenitors (<citation rid="DMM034637C8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.34110" pmcid="PMC6025960" pmid="29956664" count="1">Eley et al., 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, changes in NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cell distribution are also observed in the <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> model, emphasizing the importance of correct cell lineage distributions during valve formation. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the cellular dynamics of the NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF population during OFT development observed in this study suggest that these cells do not originate from the myocardial wall as proposed by <citation rid="DMM034637C28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.24641" pmid="29920846" pmcid="PMC6105448" count="1">Mifflin et al. (2018)</citation> but rather migrate from the extracardiac pool of SHF cells into the OFT cushions, in agreement with <citation rid="DMM034637C8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.34110" pmcid="PMC6025960" pmid="29956664" count="1">Eley et al. (2018)</citation>. <sentence_start/>However, the 3D reconstructions developed in our study do not indicate the formation of a detached/isolated developing intercalated cushion as the transitional zone did not develop into the NC or NF leaflets of the aortic and pulmonary valve. <sentence_start/>The transitional zones did not experience cushion swelling by cellularization as observed in the parietal and septal cushions but remained a thin region of cardiac jelly connecting the parietal and septal cushions during development. <sentence_start/>The development of the NC and NF from the septal and parietal cushions is further supported by the observations of the NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cells as a distinct group within the parietal and septal cushion that eventually develop into the NC and NF leaflets of the aortic and pulmonary valve, respectively.

The asymmetric contribution of the NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> population to the aortic and pulmonary poles of the OFT has been described as the pulmonary push concept (<citation rid="DMM034637C38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dvdy.23833" pmid="22826212" count="1">Scherptong et al., 2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>The greater number of contributing SHF cells to the pulmonary pole of the OFT in relation to that of the aortic pole might explain the susceptibility of <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos to develop BAV as opposed to bicuspid pulmonary valve. <sentence_start/>The difference in cellular distribution within the pulmonary valve could possibly not reflect that of the aortic valve and could therefore be affected differently by the <italic>Nos3</italic> mutation. <sentence_start/>This subtle difference in cell lineage distribution might underlie the rarity of a bicuspid pulmonary valve in both mice and humans.

Our observations of cushion invagination for valve formation has also been reported in the vertebrate zebrafish model, suggesting a conserved mechanism for leaflet separation (<citation rid="DMM034637C39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dev.010694" pmid="18272595" count="1">Scherz et al., 2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Whether the process of leaflet separation is the result of active endothelial invasion or a result of passive geometric rearrangement, e.g. by outgrowth of the valvular leaflets, is yet to be determined.

NOS3 is a key mediator in the production of nitric oxide (NO) in endothelial cells and plays a role in regulating vascular tone through the L-arginine-NO pathway (<citation rid="DMM034637C35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1055/s-0038-1646156" pmid="7694388" count="1">Radomski and Moncada, 1993</citation>). <sentence_start/>Disruptions in the endothelial NO pathway have been associated with BAV in humans (<citation rid="DMM034637C18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.athoracsur.2016.04.001" pmid="27283108" pmcid="PMC6124889" count="1">Kotlarczyk et al., 2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the role of NO in OFT formation has not been studied in great detail. <sentence_start/>Signalling pathway analysis in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> mice identified abnormal EMT as a cause for BAV (<citation rid="DMM034637C9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jacc.2009.07.044" pmid="19958967" count="1">Fernández et al., 2009</citation>; <citation rid="DMM034637C23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0077611" pmid="24204893" pmcid="PMC3812218" count="1">Liu et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, these studies did not perform lineage tracing experiments and primarily relied on indirect measurements of EMT. <sentence_start/>We used <italic>Tie2Cre;mTmG</italic> mice to genetically label the endothelial-derived cells and showed that the endocardial contribution to the developing leaflets was not affected in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> animals. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the <italic>Nos3</italic> mutation did impact cell lineage distribution of neural crest and SHF cells among the leaflets of the aortic valve. <sentence_start/>This suggest that NOS3 might have an active role in guiding cell migration during development. <sentence_start/>Both SHF and neural crest cells migrate over the aortic and pulmonary arteries, in close proximity to endothelial cells. <sentence_start/>There have been reports that interactions between endothelial-derived cells and neural crest cell lineages are required for correct leaflet development (<citation rid="DMM034637C51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.111.245035" pmid="21597012" pmcid="PMC3132827" count="1">Wu et al., 2011</citation>).

Neural crest cells have been reported to be essential for correct positioning of the developing outflow cushions and patterning of the arterial valve leaflets (<citation rid="DMM034637C32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/cvr/cvt132" pmid="23723064" pmcid="PMC3718324" count="1">Phillips et al., 2013</citation>). <sentence_start/>More recently, <citation rid="DMM034637C1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1242/dmm.029710" pmid="28714851" pmcid="PMC5611965" count="1">Aghajanian et al. (2017)</citation> showed that endothelial Pdgfrα is an important factor for coordinating neural crest cell migration. <sentence_start/>The importance of correct lineage distributions of SHF, endothelial and neural crest cells in BAV formation has also been suggested by other researchers (<citation rid="DMM034637C14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI44244" pmid="21157040" pmcid="PMC3007154" count="1">Jain et al., 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>The findings presented here support the notion that misregulation of these cell lineages can result in a BAV in mice.

The angular differences in the aortic and pulmonary valve plane between wild-type, <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> TAV and <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> BAV mutants as a result of lineage defects are likely to alter normal flow patterns. <sentence_start/>There is wide support that hemodynamic aberrations contribute to the aortopathy observed in many cases of BAV (<citation rid="DMM034637C33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2017.00441" pmcid="PMC5483483" pmid="28694784" count="1">Piatti et al., 2017</citation>).

To examine the exact molecular pathways responsible for the signalling role of <italic>Nos3</italic> in influencing neural crest and SHF distribution in OFT development, further research is required. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the advent of RNA-sequencing can shed light on the molecular mechanisms involved in cellular communication among early cell lineages.
Conclusion

During OFT development, the parietal endocardial cushion gives rise to the RC and NC leaflets of the aortic valve as well as to the RF leaflet of the pulmonary valve. <sentence_start/>The septal cushion gives rise to the LC leaflet of the aortic valve as well as the LF and NF leaflets of the pulmonary valve. <sentence_start/>This asymmetric leaflet formation leads to non-uniform cell lineage distributions in the aortic valve. <sentence_start/>The non-coronary aortic leaflet is primarily populated by NKX2.5<sup>+</sup>/TM<sup>−</sup> SHF cells, whereas neural-crest-derived cells primarily populate the RC and LC aortic leaflets. <sentence_start/>Endothelial-derived cell populations contribute to each leaflet equally. <sentence_start/>However, <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos develop BAV due to defects in endothelial-linked separation of the parietal cushion into the NC and RC aortic leaflet accompanied by a different pattern of disposition of embryonic cell lineages. <sentence_start/>All <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos show increased contributions of SHF cells to the NC and LC leaflets, while a reduction of neural crest cells is observed in the RC leaflet. <sentence_start/>Moreover, embryonic lineage defects involved in valve formation result in morphometric changes of the OFT leading to aberrant positioning of the aortic and pulmonary valve in both tricuspid and bicuspid <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos, although it is more pronounced in the latter. <sentence_start/>These valve alignment anomalies are most probably the result of aberrations in neural-crest-derived AP-septum formation in <italic>Nos3<sup>−/−</sup></italic> embryos. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that differences in early neural crest and SHF lineage distributions, as seen in BAV, are not limited solely to valve formation but impact complete cardiac OFT development.
